abstract: This paper describes the application of the variable structure control (VSC) concept for dc motor position control. The control scheme is derived, implemented, and tested in the laboratory where both digital and analog controllers have been used to control a representative servo system. The control-system schematics are given and sample results are shown for illustration. The VSC experiment should be of interest to educators and design engineers who wish to demonstrate and investigate sophisticated position-control methods and their applications. This experiment may also serve as a basis for further applications of VSC.

articleTitle: Automatic solution of optimal control problems III: Differential and integral constraints
abstract: An automatic method for obtaining the numerical solution of a certain class of second-order nonlinear optimal control problems with differential and integral constraints is described. The nonlinear two-point boundary value problem is solved using the Newton-Raphson method for obtaining successive approximations of the solution. The derivatives required for the solution of the problem are computed automatically using the table method. The user of the program need only input the integrand of the cost functional and the differential constraints and specify the intial conditions and the terminal time. None of the derivatives usually associated with Pontryagin's maximum principle and the Newton-Raphson method need be calculated by hand. A set of FORTRAN subroutines in the program for solving the optimal control problems is described. An example is given with numerical results.

articleTitle: Recollections of the early development of servomechanisms and control systems
History of personal involvment in feedback control theory
On-line order selection and parameter estimation--An experimental application
abstract: The experimental application of an integrated on-line order determination and a parameter estimation algorithm to a storage plant is presented. The experiments are carried out on different operating points around which the plant can be modeled as a linear, discrete-time, stochastic and S.I.S.O. system. A simple algorithm for the determination of the order is proposed. The experiment is based on testing recursively the significance of the reduction in the prediction error variance when increasing the model order, by means of a modified F-test. The results of three well-known identification procedures, used to perform the parameter estimation in different conditions, are also reported for comparison purposes.

articleTitle: Eigenvalue assignments for large-scale discrete systems containing delayed interconnections: A two-level control
abstract: A two-level control scheme is utilized to satisfy eigenvalue assignments for discrete-time, delayed interconnected systems. A preliminary feedback is applied to minimize the interconnections' effect. It is then shown that the perturbations of the interconnections during operation is equivalent to the creation of a higher hierarchical level that accounts for such disruptions. Conditions are derived for connective assignability, that is, for preserving the same eigenvalues and eigenvectors despite certain perturbations of the interconnections during operation.

articleTitle: A control systems laboratory with microcomputer supervision
abstract: An introductory control systems laboratory is presented which uses a microcomputer to provide an automated and highly flexible set of experiments. Most of the important theoretical concepts which are presented in an introductory course in control systems are illustrated through experiments on an electro-mechanical system. These experiments provide students with a physical insight into the theory.

articleTitle: DESIRE: A new interactive simulation systems for control system applications
abstract: DESIRE is a new interactive simulation system for minicomputers. DESIRE is exceptionally convenient for modelling new control systems because, unlike earlier continuous-system simulation systems, it executes directly on a RUN command and still runs 1.3 to 5 times faster than minicomputer Fortran. Experimenters can see effects of system as well as parameter changes without noticeable translation delays. Examples of control system applications include interactive simulation of a nonlinear servo, iterative parameter optimization, matrix operations, and especially efficient simulation of continuous-variable plants with digital controllers.

articleTitle: Digital control of an unstable plant
abstract: An unstable third-order system is controlled digitally by pole-assignment technique and observer theory. The unstable plant is simulated on an EAI 680 analog computer, and a DEC-10 minicomputer is used to implement the controller. The minimum sampling rate required for stable operation is determined.

articleTitle: Some comments on reduction of parameter variations by use of feedback
abstract: Two formulae regarding reduction of output variation of an elementary feedback system due to variations in system parameters are derived and discussed. Certain confusing and often erroneously treated aspects are detailed and illustrated.

articleTitle: Nicholas Minorsky and the automatic steering of ships
History and development of dynamic programming
abstract: The development of DP (dynamic programming) is presented in a chronological order. Although it seems awkward, it does show that science never develops in a correct and straightforward fashion. It is only afterwards that a scientific development can be made logical and rational. The emphasis is placed on the actual development of DP and its interconnections with other basic areas, such as invariant imbedding. Another area of emphasis is the possible future research directions. Most of the detailed derivations and equations are omitted.

abstract: This is the first of a two-part series based on a roundtable discussion held at the 21st IEEE Conference on Decision and Control and organized by the Control Systems Society Professional Activities Committee. Part I is based on prepared statements by the first five roundtable participants, while Part II is based on Leo Fanning's review of the activities of the IEEE Washington Office in the areas of technology policy.
